name: Loma (Liberia)
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: Mishchenko 2017 §2.1.2: «Ударение в Л.я. отсутствует. Противопоставляются два уровневых фонетических тона, низкий и высокий: pà ‛приходить’, pá ‛убивать’. Носителем фонетического тона является слог. Сегментным носителем фонологического тона, или тонемы, является морфема.» || Dwyer 1981 §3.35 (Liberian Lorma): "Lorma is a syllable-timed language. This means that every syllable has the same duration as every other one (long vowels are considered to be two syllables). In English this is not the case because English is a stress-timed language." || Dwyer 1981 App. E.2: "While stress is generally non-contrastive in Mande it is generally distinctive. In Kpelle, it falls on the first high-toned syllable in the word, or if the word has no high tones, it falls on the first syllable."
new_statements.translation: Mishchenko: 'There is no stress in the Looma language. Two level phonetic tones are contrasted, low and high: pà "come", pá "kill". The bearer of phonetic tone is the syllable. The segmental bearer of phonological tone, or toneme, is the morpheme.'

This means that every syllable has the same duration as every other one (long vowels are considered to be two…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Looma is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with no word stress; the Liberian-specific handbook adds only that Lorma is syllable-timed (all syllables of equal duration) and gives a generic Mande/Kpelle stress rule (first H-toned syllable, else first syllable) without asserting it for Lorma. No Liberian Loma source opened states a word-stress position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None as a rule; Sadler 1949/2006 p.21 incidentally notes that in taɣa-i 'the nest' 'the second syllable receives more stress' when the definite suffix -i is added (a one-word remark, not a system statement).
new_statements.domain_note: Mishchenko's statement is about the word-prosodic system (tone-bearing unit = syllable, toneme domain = morpheme/foot). Dwyer's remark concerns rhythm/timing at sentence level. Empirical base of the explicit 'no stress' statement is Guinean Woi-Balagha (toma1245), though the article's object language includes the Liberian dialects.
new_statements.first_reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.identity_note: The only explicit word-stress statement found (Mishchenko 2017, 'no stress') is from a whole-language encyclopedia article on Looma (Guinea + Liberia) whose data base is the Guinean Woi-Balagha dialect (= Glottolog toma1245, Toma); the article lists the Liberian dialects (Wubomai, Gbunde, Ziema, Briama, Zozo, Gizima) as part of its object language and does not flag stress as dialect-specific. The Liberian-specific descriptions opened (Sadler 1949/2006, Woozie, N. Liberia; Dwyer 1981a,b, Liberian Lorma/Gbunde; Vydrine 1989 after Sadler; Rude 1983, Zenalomai speaker) describe two tones and are silent on word stress except Dwyer's 'syllable-timed' note and Sadler's incidental remark.

sources.citation: Sadler, Wesley. 2006 [ms. 1949]. A Complete Analysis of the Lɔɔma Language, Interior Liberia, West Africa (ed. V. Vydrine). Mandenkan 42: 1-109. (= Sadler's 1949 Hartford thesis; Liberian Loma)
sources.note: Ch. I 'Pronunciation' covers phonemes, vowel length (1.3, phonemic), nasalisation (1.6), tone (1.7 -> Ch. V: 'There are two tones in Lɔɔma, high and low'), syllable patterns (1.8); no word-stress/accent section at all. Only an incidental remark p.21 sec. 1.10.1 on taɣa 'nest': 'When the definite suffix /-i/ is added, the second syllable receives more stress, and /ɣ/ is used by most speakers.'
